summary: A failover plan now tells you whether the spare can actually carry the cameras, not just whether it can reach them. Testing a plan used to answer one question — can the standby appliance open these cameras — and stayed silent on the other one, which is whether it could record them all at once. The control plane now asks the spare itself how many cameras it reckons it can handle, counts the ones it is already recording of its own, adds anything other plans have pointed at the same spare, and says plainly whether it fits, only just fits, or does not. A plan that does not fit will not be called ready, however well its test went. What it will still do is take the cameras over anyway when a recorder dies: being over the estimate means dropped frames, and nothing recording at all is the one outcome that cannot be undone afterwards — so you are told, loudly, in the alert and in the trail, and the takeover proceeds.
compatibility: Additive, and nothing about existing plans changes except that they now say more. Existing plans pick the figure up the next time they are staged or tested; until then they say the spare has not been asked, which is honest rather than alarming. An appliance too old to answer the question also reads as not asked, and that never blocks a plan that has otherwise been tested — otherwise upgrading the control plane would quietly un-protect every older recorder. Creating a plan is never refused on capacity grounds: the figure is an estimate the appliance itself labels as one, and leaving somebody with no plan rather than a plan with a warning on it would be worse. The estimate is what the spare says it can do, not a measurement of what it will do under load.
